slides.title: You've been running at 100%.
slides.content: And calling it living. Success was supposed to be the finish line, not just the beginning of a race we never chose.
slides.notes: Hold up the mirror. Name the exhaustion of the urban trap. The average professional spends less than 2% outdoors.
slides.narrationText:
You’ve been running at 100%... and calling it living. That’s the strange part — not that people are tired, but that exhaustion has become the operating system. Success was supposed to be the finish line, uhm, not a race that never seems to end.

Most people in cities spend less than 2% of their time outdoors. Think about what that means: almost all your waking hours are spent under fluorescent light, in traffic, in rooms that ask more from you than they give back. The body adapts, sure. The nervous system does too. But adaptation isn’t the same as health. It’s just what happens when you stay in one gear for too long. And after a while, even the good parts of life start to feel like another item on the list.

Well, that’s the real trap. Not hard work itself — it’s the absence of any rhythm that tells you when to come down. You keep performing at a level that was never meant to be permanent, then wonder why rest feels unfamiliar. The cost isn’t only fatigue. It’s that your attention gets thinner, your patience shortens, and the day starts to feel like something you survive instead of inhabit.

So this is the first honest question: what if the problem isn’t that you need to do more? What if you need a different pattern altogether? Because once you see that, the next question becomes unavoidable — what does protecting a part of your year actually look like?

slides.title: “You can get very good at a life that is quietly hurting you.”
slides.narrationText: You can get very good at a life that is quietly hurting you.

slides.title: What if 10% was enough?
slides.content: 30 nights a year in the deep quiet of the wilderness. Enough time to reset your circadian rhythm. Not subtraction — protection.
slides.notes: Explain the 10% solution: 30 nights annually. A practice, not a holiday. The math of transformation.
slides.narrationText:
And that’s the strange part... ten percent is not a loss. It’s the thing that keeps the rest from collapsing into noise.

Thirty nights a year is enough to do real work on a nervous system that’s been running hot for too long. Not a symbolic visit. Not a one-off exhale. A recurring return to deep quiet, where your body starts remembering its own timing again. uhm, circadian rhythm sounds clinical until you feel what happens when it comes back online — sleep gets cleaner, attention gets steadier, the edges soften. This is why the number matters. Thirty nights is small enough to protect and large enough to change the pattern. It’s not subtraction... it’s protection. You’re not taking time away from your life. You’re defending the part of your year that makes the rest of it workable.

And once you see it that way, the whole idea of rest changes. It stops being something you squeeze in after the damage is done. It becomes a practice you keep. A rhythm you return to before the noise accumulates again. Well, that’s the difference between relief and recalibration.

So the real question isn’t whether you can spare 10%. It’s whether you can afford not to protect it. Because the other 90% doesn’t stay strong by accident... it gets stronger when something quiet is held in reserve.

And that’s where the proof has to come in. Once the frame makes sense, you start asking whether it actually works in the world.

slides.title: Seven years of quiet work.
slides.content: 6 collectives. 1,300 acres. 250 families. We didn't just find land — we restore it. Earn trust with substance.
slides.notes: Six collectives. 1,300 acres. 250 families. Seven years. Each number as its own sentence. Regeneration, not development.
slides.narrationText:
Seven years changes the meaning of a number. Six collectives, 1,300 acres, 250 families... those aren’t marketing claims. They’re the residue of work that kept going when nobody was clapping.

Uhm, that matters because land doesn’t respond to intent alone. It responds to seasons, to labor, to patience, to people staying long enough to mend what had been broken. Beforest didn’t arrive, point at a map, and call it a collective. It worked across degraded ground, brought it back into use, and kept restoring while the rest of the world was still talking about sustainability as an idea. Six collectives means six places where that discipline has taken root. 1,300 acres means the effort is spatial, not symbolic. And 250 families... well, that tells you this has crossed from a private project into a shared way of living.

See, trust doesn’t come from language this clean. It comes from substance. From whether the work holds up after the brochure is gone. From whether families return, whether the land improves, whether the system can carry real people without collapsing into performance.

And that changes the whole frame. You’re not being asked to believe in a concept. You’re being invited into something already in motion, already tested, already carrying weight. That’s a different kind of confidence. Quieter. Harder to fake.

So the real question becomes simple: if the work is already this far along, what does your own place in it look like?

slides.title: “Rest is not a reward. It is a rhythm worth protecting.”
slides.narrationText: Rest is not a reward. It is a rhythm worth protecting.

slides.title: Rewilded landscapes by Beforest.
slides.content: Poomaale 1.0 & 2.0, Coorg · Hammiyala, Coorg · Hyderabad · Bhopal · Mumbai. Belonging to a place, not just visiting.
slides.notes: Showcase the sanctuaries. Ancient forests, coffee plantations, grasslands. Not amenities — transformation.
slides.narrationText:
These aren’t properties. They’re thresholds.

Poomaale, Hammiyala, Hyderabad, Bhopal, Mumbai... each one holds a different kind of silence, and a different kind of work. In Coorg, you move through ancient forest canopy, coffee, cardamom, mist. At Hammiyala, the land opens into coffee agroforestry and high-altitude grasslands, with fireflies at night. Hyderabad sits on the Deccan plateau, with old rock and scrub that feel almost geological in their patience. And then there’s Mumbai, where silence has to be earned because the city never really stops pressing in.

That’s the point, uhm. You’re not being offered a polished retreat with a few trees around it. You’re being invited into landscapes that were restored, held, and made habitable again. Belonging here means your time starts to take the shape of the land — slower in some places, sharper in others, but always more honest. Beforest doesn’t treat nature as decoration. It treats it as a place where your nervous system can remember its own pace. And because these are collectives, not isolated hideaways, the meaning changes again: you’re not passing through. You’re entering a rhythm that already has other people in it.

That matters because most urban life keeps you slightly outside everything, even when you’re inside a room. Here, you’re not consuming a scene. You’re participating in a landscape that has already been brought back from neglect. That changes how you rest, how you arrive, how long you stay after your first evening quietens down.

And once that lands, the next question is obvious... what does it actually mean to make this part of your year?

slides.title: 300 Nights of Intentional Living.
slides.content: 30 person-nights per year for 10 years. Across all Beforest Collectives. Access, not ownership. No carry-forward — rhythm, not accumulation.
slides.notes: Address objections directly. Person-nights, not family nights. Frame it as a recurring reset practice.
slides.narrationText:
And that’s the part that usually makes people pause... because the structure is where the commitment becomes real. Thirty person-nights a year for ten years sounds simple until you start asking what it actually means in practice.

It means access across all Beforest Collectives. Coorg, Hyderabad, the places that are already working, already restored, already alive. You are not buying land. You are buying a rhythm of return. Uhm... that matters, because ownership asks you to manage a place, while access asks you to keep coming back to one. The difference is quiet, but it changes everything. This is person-nights, not family nights — so the unit is the individual, with room for immediate family to participate when it makes sense. And no, the nights do not carry forward. That is not a limitation. That is the point. Rhythm only works when it is lived on time.

See, accumulation is how most things get distorted. You hoard credits, then you stop moving. You protect a practice, though, and it stays alive. That’s what this is doing over ten years: giving you a protected fraction of your year that keeps resetting your system instead of becoming another thing to manage.

And uhm... that changes the feeling completely. You stop treating rest like a rare event you have to earn. You start treating it like maintenance for the part of you that has to keep functioning. That’s the real structure here.

So the question becomes simpler: if the shape is this clear, why wait to feel it in your hands?

slides.title: “You decide with your feet, not your eyes.”
slides.narrationText: You decide with your feet, not your eyes.

slides.title: The weight of 'Next Year'.
slides.content: Every year you wait is a year of 10% you don't get back. This isn't about missing an opportunity; it's about missing a version of yourself.
slides.notes: Move away from sales urgency. Focus on the personal cost of waiting. Calibration and reset are needed now, not eventually.
slides.narrationText:
Uhm... because once you understand what 10% is, the delay starts to feel heavier than the decision. Every year you say “next year” is a year you spend without that reset, without that rhythm, without the version of you that actually comes back restored.

Well, the loss here isn’t abstract. It isn’t just a missed stay, or a missed season in Coorg, or a missed month under that canopy of coffee and cardamom. It’s the slow accumulation of another year spent at full stretch, where work keeps taking and your own recovery keeps getting postponed. And the thing is... your life doesn’t wait politely for the right moment to recalibrate. The pressure keeps building, the calendar keeps filling, and the part of you that needed protection gets pushed further back. So the cost of waiting is not just time. It’s momentum in the wrong direction.

Right, and that matters because exhaustion has a way of becoming normal when you leave it alone long enough. You stop noticing how much energy it takes to be “fine.” You start calling strain a routine. This is why 10% is not a nice-to-have. It’s a boundary. A protected rhythm that stops the rest of the year from hardening around stress.

And if that’s true... then the real question isn’t whether you can do this someday. It’s whether you want another year to pass before you feel the difference.

slides.title: Blyton Bungalow: The First 1%.
slides.content: Experience before commitment. A Kodava-inspired sanctuary built from the earth. 128 acres of private coffee forest in Coorg.
slides.notes: Details: Hospitality without the footprint. 6 signature rooms in Poomaale 1.0 where we are conserving 60 million liters of water. A place where 90-point coffee is grown. The pilot, not the backup plan. Every rupee of the trial stay will be adjusted towards membership.
slides.narrationText:
This is where it stops being an idea and becomes a place you can actually stand in. Blyton Bungalow is not the polished finish line... it’s the first 1%, the part that lets you feel the thing before you commit to living by it.

Well, there’s a reason this matters. It sits in 128 acres of private coffee forest in Coorg, built in a Kodava register, from the earth, not against it. Six signature rooms in Poomaale 1.0, with hospitality that leaves almost no footprint, while 60 million liters of water are being conserved in the same landscape. That’s the point... the experience is not separate from the ethic. Even the coffee here is part of the story — 90-point coffee grown on land that is being cared for, not consumed. And the trial itself is honest. You come in, you experience it, and every rupee from that stay adjusts toward membership if you choose to join.

So what that means is simple: you are not being asked to believe first. You’re being asked to feel the rhythm first. That changes the whole shape of the decision. It takes the pressure off the mind and puts the truth back in the body, where it usually belongs. Uhm... and once you’ve felt that, the rest gets clearer very quickly.

Right... this is why the first step matters more than the pitch. The land will tell you what the slide can’t.

You decide with your feet, not your eyes. See you in the slow lane.
